text: Raspberry Pi OS is a Unix-like operating system developed for the Raspberry Pi line of single-board computers and is based on Debian, a Linux distribution. It is maintained by Raspberry Pi Holdings and optimized for the Pi's hardware, featuring low memory requirements and support for both 32-bit and 64-bit architectures. Originally released in July 2012 under the name Raspbian, it followed the launch of the first Raspberry Pi model. Raspbian was initially developed by Mike Thompson and Peter Green as an independent and unofficial port of Debian to the Raspberry Pi, with the first build released on 15 July 2012. At the time, the Raspberry Pi had no official operating system, so the Raspberry Pi Foundation built upon the Raspbian project and began releasing its own operating system images, with the first official release of Raspbian announced on 10 September 2013. On 28 May 2020, the Foundation announced a beta 64-bit version based on Debian's user space software, not Raspbian. To avoid confusion, the name of the official operating system images was changed to Raspberry Pi OS, a change applied to both 32-bit and 64-bit versions, though the 64-bit version remained based on Raspbian. The 64-bit version of Raspberry Pi OS was officially released on 2 February 2022. The user interface is optimized for Raspberry Pi hardware, with low base memory requirements, aiming for a lightweight, fast, and energy-efficient desktop experience. It is built on the Wayland display protocol using labwc as its compositing manager, which is based on wlroots. The system previously used the X Window System, transitioning to Wayland starting with the Bullseye release in 2021, which introduced mutter to support both X and Wayland, and in the Bookworm release of 2023, wayfire was adopted as a dedicated Wayland compositor. Performance issues on older models led to a search for a better alternative, and in 2024, labwc was selected as a lightweight compositor that matches the hardware's capabilities, now offering performance comparable to X across all models, making Wayland the default. The interface is designed to feel familiar to users of macOS and Microsoft Windows, featuring a top menu bar with an application menu, shortcuts, and system controls like Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, volume, and clock. Raspberry Pi OS originally included the Epiphany web browser, which was replaced by Chromium in 2016, and Firefox was added as a pre-installed browser in 2023. Both browsers come with uBlock and h264ify extensions. As of May 2025, other pre-installed applications include Geany, ImageMagick, Thonny, VNC Viewer, and VLC media player. Installations with the full suite of recommended software include Claws Mail, Firebird database server, KiCad, LibreOffice, Java, Scratch, Wolfram Mathematica, and additional font packages. Software can be installed via the APT command-line interface, through the Add/Remove Software tool, or via third-party app stores like Pi-Apps. According to Raspberry Pi Imager usage statistics, Raspberry Pi OS accounted for 67% of all operating system downloads for the Raspberry Pi in May 2025, followed by Ubuntu at 9%. In a 2015 review, Jesse Smith of DistroWatch noted that Raspbian was not well-suited for heavier desktop workloads but provided a functional experience with a lightweight environment, being responsive with a modest number of applications but struggling with resource-intensive software like LibreOffice or Firefox. In a January 2024 review for Ars Technica, Andrew Cunningham tested Raspberry Pi OS 12 (Bookworm) on a Pi 5 with 8 GB of RAM and found it functional for general-purpose desktop use, though it lacked modern features such as window snapping, a notification center, refined window borders, and smooth multi-monitor performance, and had limited native app availability for ARM Linux, often requiring web-based versions of services like Slack, Zoom, and Dropbox. In January 2021, the raspberrypi-sys-mods package added a Microsoft GPG encryption key and repository configuration to enable easier installation of Visual Studio Code, prompting privacy concerns due to Microsoft’s past adversarial stance in the open source community; the configuration was later removed. Raspberry Pi OS is available in three main variants: standard, Lite (without a desktop environment), and Full (with a desktop and recommended software), each available in both 32-bit and 64-bit versions. A "legacy" branch has been available since December 2021, based on the previous stable release of Debian, allowing continued use of older software while receiving security and hardware support updates. All standard variants are offered in this legacy form. New major versions of Debian are released every two years, typically in the summer of odd-numbered years (e.g., 2023, 2025, 2027), and Raspberry Pi OS ports generally follow a few months later, usually in the fall. The operating system can be purchased pre-installed on a microSD card or downloaded as a .img disk image file to be written to an SD card or other media. Official documentation recommends a minimum of 16 GB for the Lite version and at least 32 GB for versions with a desktop environment. The Raspberry Pi Imager utility, introduced in March 2020, simplifies the installation of a disk image file onto an SD card or other media and is available for macOS, Raspberry Pi OS, Ubuntu, and Windows, allowing users to download and write the image in a single application. It also supports a variety of third-party operating systems.
